name: image/apng
description:
APNG extends PNG with animation. It adds a control chunk and a sequence of frame chunks, all placed in chunk types a plain PNG decoder is required to skip. The first frame is a complete, valid PNG image, so software that does not understand APNG shows a still picture rather than failing.

That backwards compatibility is why it replaced GIF for short loops on the web. It offers full 8-bit alpha and 24-bit colour instead of a 256-colour palette and 1-bit transparency.

It began as a Mozilla extension. It was later registered with IANA and folded into the W3C PNG specification. The older Mozilla-era label is at [image/vnd.mozilla.apng](/image/vnd.mozilla.apng).

name: image/jxs
description:
JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122) is a low-latency, visually lossless codec. It is designed around the opposite trade to most codecs: it compresses only modestly, but does so in a fraction of a frame. End-to-end latency is measured in scanlines rather than frames.

That makes it a mezzanine format rather than a delivery one. It carries near-uncompressed video over links that cannot carry raw pixels. That is how it reached ST 2110-22, the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers standard for professional video over IP. RFC 9134 defines the matching RTP payload format.

`image/jxs` labels the file form; the bare codestream is [image/jxsc](/image/jxsc).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9134 - RTP Payload Format for ISO/IEC 21122 (JPEG XS)

name: image/jxsc
description:
A bare JPEG XS codestream (ISO/IEC 21122), without the file structure that [image/jxs](/image/jxs) provides. It is the form sent over a professional video-over-IP link, where the transport already carries timing and format information.

The IANA registry lists further JPEG XS types for carriage inside ISO base media containers, which this site does not document yet.

name: image/avci
description:
AVCI is a still image coded with AVC (H.264) and stored in the HEIF container defined by ISO/IEC 23008-12. HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format, is the same container used by [image/heif](/image/heif) and [image/heic](/image/heic). This type commits to AVC rather than HEVC.

It exists because the HEIF container design is codec-agnostic by intent, and the media type is how a file declares which codec is inside. It is far rarer than HEIC, because the devices that adopted HEIF adopted HEVC, High Efficiency Video Coding, along with it.

The image sequence form is [image/avcs](/image/avcs).

name: image/avcs
description:
The image sequence counterpart to [image/avci](/image/avci). It holds several AVC-coded images in one HEIF container (ISO/IEC 23008-12), for bursts, animations and derived sequences rather than a single still. HEIF is the High Efficiency Image File Format.

A sequence is carried as a track rather than a lone item. That is why the registration takes its encoding considerations from `video/mp4`, and expects the first entry of a `codecs` parameter to name a track with the `pict` handler.

It stands to `image/avci` as [image/heic-sequence](/image/heic-sequence) stands to [image/heic](/image/heic).

name: image/ktx
description:
KTX is the Khronos texture container: a thin wrapper around texture data that is already in a GPU-native compressed format. It also carries the mipmap chain, array layers and cube map faces.

The point is that the file needs no transcoding at load time. An engine reads the header and passes the payload straight to OpenGL or Vulkan, and the GPU uses it as it stands. [image/png](/image/png) and [image/jpeg](/image/jpeg) must instead be decoded to raw pixels and recompressed before they are useful as textures.

Version 2 is a separate media type, [image/ktx2](/image/ktx2).

name: image/ktx2
description:
KTX 2.0 is the second version of the Khronos texture container. It addresses the problem that made [image/ktx](/image/ktx) awkward to ship: GPU texture formats are not portable, so a KTX 1 file had to be built for each target platform.

KTX 2.0 adds Basis Universal supercompression. Textures are stored in an intermediate form that transcodes cheaply, at load time, to whichever block format the device supports. One file serves every GPU.

glTF consumes it through the `KHR_texture_basisu` extension, which is where most people encounter it.

name: model/gltf+json
description:
glTF (GL Transmission Format) is the Khronos Group's runtime format for 3D scenes and models. It is built for delivery rather than authoring. A file holds the scene graph, materials and animations, and points at binary buffers of geometry that an engine can hand to the GPU with almost no processing.

That focus on load time is why it is often called the JPEG of 3D: a format for delivering finished assets rather than for editing them. This type is the JSON form, which references its buffers and textures as separate files. Everything packed into a single binary container is [model/gltf-binary](/model/gltf-binary).

name: model/gltf-binary
description:
GLB is the single-file form of glTF. It has the same JSON scene description, with its binary buffers and textures packed into one container behind a short header. Nothing has to be fetched separately, which makes it the practical choice for shipping a model over a network.

Textures inside a GLB are often Basis Universal supercompressed and carried as [image/ktx2](/image/ktx2), through the KHR_texture_basisu extension. The form that keeps its buffers as separate files is [model/gltf+json](/model/gltf+json).

name: image/vnd.valve.source.texture
description:
VTF, the Valve Texture Format, is the texture format of Valve's Source engine, used by Half-Life 2, Portal, Team Fortress 2 and the games and mods built on them. A file holds the image data along with its mipmaps, flags and any animation frames the engine expects.

VTF files are almost always paired with a `.vmt` material script. That script tells the engine which shader to use and how to interpret the texture. On its own a VTF file is only pixels.
